definition.text: An interaction in which one organism, the predator, kills and eats another, its prey.

facts.text: Predation belongs to a family of feeding behaviours with parasitism and parasitoidism, and overlaps with herbivory when animals destroy seeds.
To feed, a predator must search for, pursue and kill its prey, weighing costs and benefits at each step.
Predators affect ecosystems indirectly too, by changing herbivore behaviour, as wolves do for riverside vegetation and sea otters for kelp forests.
Predators can raise biodiversity by stopping any one species from becoming dominant; such predators are called keystone species.
Without predators a prey population can grow exponentially until it nears carrying capacity; predators limit prey by eating them and changing their behaviour.
Predator–prey interactions may explain population cycles such as those of lynx and snowshoe hares.

definition.text: The ways predators search for and capture prey, from sit-and-wait ambush to active chase.

facts.text: Sit-and-wait suits dense, mobile prey and low energy needs; wide foraging costs more energy and suits sparse or sedentary prey.
In social predation, groups such as wolves or hyenas cooperate to kill animals as large as buffalo.
Specialists such as the Eurasian lynx hunt few prey types, while generalists such as leopards take at least 100 species.

definition.text: The arms race in which predators and prey evolve adaptations that counter each other.

facts.text: Bats evolved echolocation to find insects, and some insects evolved the ability to hear those calls.
Prey defences include camouflage, mimicry and warning others of predators.

definition.text: The rate at which an ecosystem makes new biomass, often measured in grams per square metre per day.

facts.text: Productivity of plants and other autotrophs is primary productivity; that of animals and other heterotrophs is secondary productivity.
It depends on nutrient availability, temperature and water availability.
Swamps and marshes are listed as producing 2,500 gC/m²/yr of biomass.
Fertilizer nutrients can trigger algal blooms that raise primary production but make the ecosystem less stable.

definition.text: Gross primary production is all the carbon producers fix into organic matter; net primary production is what remains after they use some for their own respiration.

facts.text: NPP is calculated as gross primary production minus respiration.
Most primary production comes from photosynthesis, using sunlight, water and CO2.
Where there is no light, as in groundwater, caves and hydrothermal vents, lithoautotrophs using chemicals such as hydrogen sulfide or methane are the only producers.
Net ecosystem production subtracts the respiration of both autotrophs and heterotrophs from gross primary production.

definition.text: The creation of new biomass by consumers, such as animals, fungi and many bacteria, from the food they assimilate.

facts.text: It is driven by the transfer of organic material between trophic levels.
It can be estimated by methods including increment summation, removal summation, the instantaneous growth method and the Allen curve method.

title: Diversity–productivity relationship

definition.text: The long-running question of how the number of plant species in an ecosystem relates to how productive it is.

facts.text: Some research finds productivity rises with diversity, partly because more species makes it likelier a highly productive one is present.
Others find a unimodal relationship; a meta-analysis of 44 studies found it unimodal in all but one.
A 1999 study of European grasslands found productivity rose with diversity and then levelled off.

contested_note: Studies disagree whether productivity rises steadily with plant diversity or peaks at intermediate diversity.

definition.text: Succession that follows an event such as fire, harvesting or a hurricane that knocks back an existing ecosystem while leaving soil and some life in place.

facts.text: It is usually faster than primary succession because soil, seeds, roots and underground plant parts survive.
After wildfire in an oak–hickory forest, annual plants come first, then grasses and pioneers, then shrubs and young trees.
Over about 150 years such a forest returns to a stable climax community resembling the one before the fire.
Succession from Imperata grassland to secondary forest raises soil carbon stocks.
Some species need fire: knobcone pine cones open only when heated by forest fires.
